According to recent reports, welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at joint EU-U.K. efforts to reverse Brexit, Russia’s latest incursions into Poland, and the future of Myanmar’s Rohingya population.

Industry observers note that ten years after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Brexit is back on the table. This time, though, London appears eager to reverse some of the barriers created by Brexit and bridge the decade-long divide between Britain and the bloc.

Recent findings suggest that at a highly anticipated EU-U.K. summit in Brussels on Friday, British and EU leaders unveiled a modest deal to begin resetting the relationship. Under the agreement, the EU and United Kingdom will realign their carbon emissions trading systems; relax restrictions on food and agricultural trade—a major win for British farmers who have long complained about tedious export paperwork; and kick-start a “youth experience” program focused on travel, study, and work.

Although these are minor changes compared to the breadth of the 2016 Brexit framework, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Friday that the deal could inject more than $22 billion into the U.K. economy in what he called the “single biggest growth measure we could take in this Parliament.”.

“Today we draw the line on a decade of drift and division by reconnecting with old friends, by building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbors and our largest market,” Burnham noted.

According to a YouGov poll published in June, a majority of Britons believe that leaving the EU was a mistake and that London should move toward rejoining the bloc. Burnham has capitalized on this discontent, ignoring warnings from Conservative and Reform UK lawmakers who are against reopening the Brexit debate.

“It’s like the emperor’s new clothes—where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth,” Burnham said on Monday ahead of the summit. “We have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years.” A National Bureau of Economic Research working paper found that by the end of 2025, Brexit had cut British GDP by 6 percent to 8 percent and investment by 12 percent to 13 percent.

According to recent reports, analysts suggest that global insecurity fueled by Russia’s war in Ukraine, the U.S. trade war, and energy market unpredictability have further convinced Britons that a post-Brexit world comes with greater instability.

“Our security and defence partnership, as well as our united support for Ukraine, are central to our commitment to address together the growing geopolitical challenges we face,” European Council President António Costa wrote on X on Friday, adding that the “EU and the UK are both stronger when we work together.”.

It is unclear how much closer the bridging of ties will go. For every step toward dismantling Brexit, Burnham is expected to face backlash back home. “This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain,” far-right Reform UK leader Niger Farage, a chief architect of the 2016 vote, said last month after Burnham floated restoring freedom of movement with the EU.

On Brussels’s side, though, the EU remains open to having “the closest possible relationship” with the United Kingdom, Costa stated.

Recent findings suggest that missile incursions. Two Russian cruise missiles and a suspected drone entered Poland on Friday, adding to the growing number of reported Russian incursions into NATO territory in recent months. The incidents occurred while Russia was carrying out a massive overnight bombardment on Ukraine.

Sources indicate that the intrusions coincided with European military exercises in Poland that began on Nov. 9; one Russian missile reportedly crashed only 22 miles from where the drills were taking place. No injuries were reported; however, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said it was “not accidental” that Russia’s incursions and the European military drills occurred in tandem. “We are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Moscow, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk added. Moscow has yet to comment.

According to Ukrainian Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, Russia’s nighttime barrage also triggered emergency outages across 11 Ukrainian regions as strikes on critical energy infrastructure forced three nuclear power plants to reduce generation. Russian attacks on Friday also reportedly hit apartment buildings, medical facilities, and bridges. Moscow’s Defense Ministry mentioned it targeted sites where weapons were being manufactured.

According to recent reports, genocide ruling. Myanmar’s military-run government on Friday denounced an International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling that found the country’s security forces guilty of genocide against its minority Rohingya Muslim community. The landmark decision, issued on Thursday, marked the first time that the court has found a country to be directly responsible for the crime.

“The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa stated during a readout of the 9-6 ruling.

Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry called the decision a “great disappointment” and noted that the judgment was not unanimous. It also said that the roughly 1.3 million Rohingya refugees in neighboring Bangladesh will only be allowed to return “when situations permit.”.

However, Tom Andrews, the former U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in Myanmar, told Foreign Policy that a 9-6 result is still a “strong majority.” But he said that the international community must take additional steps to ensure that the country’s ruling junta faces real repercussions for its actions. “Because the thing is, if we establish that there is no consequence for genocide, then we can be guaranteed that genocide is going to happen again,” Andrews said. “And it’s only by imposing consequences that we can begin to see justice prevail, not only in this case but in future cases.”.

Industry observers note that resetting relations. Chinese President Xi Jinping celebrated a “comprehensive turnaround” in his country’s relationship with Australia on Friday. Speaking on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi noted that Beijing is eager to set aside the two nations’ differences and expand cooperation in several critical sectors, such as artificial intelligence, energy, agriculture, and mining.

China is Australia’s top trading partner. However, ties between the Indo-Pacific powers began to deteriorate in 2020 after Canberra called for an inquiry into the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic, prompting China to impose punitive tariffs on Australian goods. In recent years, though, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has sought to restore bilateral relations, especially as the future of his country’s critical iron ore industry comes under threat.

Industry observers note that for decades, Chinese iron ore purchases have invigorated Australia’s economy; the vital resource was exempt from China’s 2020 duties. But with Beijing diversifying its partnerships in Africa and Latin America, where iron ore can be supplied more cheaply, as well as exercising increased leverage over iron ore pricing, Canberra is worried that its export earnings will take a major hit.

A. Kuwait B. Cyprus C. Oman D. Germany.

Industry observers note that while Trump can brag about Xi meeting him on the tarmac in Shenzhen, China, this week, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has something she can brag about from her trip, too: going viral on Chinese social media. After spending the roughly 21-hour trip from Mexico City to Shenzhen (with a stopover in Tijuana, Mexico) sitting in a middle seat on an economy flight, Sheinbaum was greeted at the airport by a military guard and a dancing troupe. But they didn’t meet her at her plane—instead, she arrived to the welcome ceremony via airport bus.

Her down-to-earth travel style seems to have appealed to many Chinese netizens: A hashtag about her arrival was seen 10 million times on the Chinese social media platform Weibo, according to Bloomberg.

The tit-for-tat strikes between Iran and the United States this week marked an end to a roughly two-month lull in such attacks, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report.

Democrat Victoria Broderick, seen here speaking to a reporter outside the Capitol on Nov. 11, has unseated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, democrat Victoria Broderick has defeated Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee’s 4th District, giving her party the 259th seat of its commanding House majority in the next Congress.

Broderick, a tech support worker, was leading by 361 votes when The Associated Press called the race Tuesday, three weeks after all votes were cast.

Industry observers note that broderick’s victory ranks among the most surprising Democratic wins of this year’s midterm elections. DesJarlais, who defeated Broderick in 2024 by more than 40 points, was not considered vulnerable heading into Election Day.

Industry observers note that but the election two years ago took place under a previous version of Tennessee’s congressional map. Following this spring’s Supreme Court ruling that limited the use of race in redistricting, the state’s Republican-led legislature redrew the House lines to eliminate Rep. Steve Cohen’s Memphis-area district, the lone seat held by Democrats.

It has been revealed that in doing so, though, the fresh map significantly altered the boundaries of the largely rural 4th District in Middle Tennessee, which now extends into Nashville’s Davidson County. Thirty-three percent of DesJarlais’ constituents were new to him, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, as the district shifted from one that Donald Trump carried by 43 points in 2024 to one that would have backed him by 24 points.

Sources indicate that under the new map, Republicans struggled to win most of the state’s House seats earlier this month. They narrowly won Cohen’s 9th District, one of just three flips for the party this year nationwide. But Broderick’s win ensures that Tennessee will continue to have a Democrat in its congressional delegation.

DesJarlais had already conceded the race before Tuesday’s AP call.

Recent findings suggest that “As the final votes have now been tabulated in this new and completely restructured district, it appears that we have a result showing my campaign has come just a few hundred votes short out of just under 200,000 votes cast,” he said in a Nov. 16 statement congratulating Broderick.

A member of the hard-line conservative Freedom Caucus, DesJarlais was first elected in 2010, unseating Democrat Lincoln Davis. While he’d been comfortably reelected in the years since, he faced competitive primaries in 2014 and 2016 after his divorce records came to light.

It has been revealed that broderick, a mother of two and a former chair of the Lincoln County Democratic Party, raised less than $100,000 for her campaign, compared with more than $650,000 for DesJarlais. She also defeated a better-funded opponent in the Democratic primary.

She told PBS NewsHour that she had essentially been campaigning for the seat since launching her 2024 bid and built relationships across the district that helped her win.

In a recent development, “I never stopped running for Congress. And when it was redistricted, I just essentially mentioned, well, the district stayed the same and actually became more competitive,” she said. “So the work's going to start speaking for itself real soon. And we saw that happen.”.

Three House races remain uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon. Louisiana will hold runoffs in December for two districts, including a Democrat-held seat that Republicans redrew in their favor. The race for Minnesota’s 1st District is heading for a hand recount, with Republican Rep. Brad Finstad trailing Democratic challenger Jake Johnson by 324 votes.

#111781. Why Israel Is Losing America

Why Israel Is Losing America

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress.
  • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Notable Ally.
  • American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Concerns on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Notable Ally.

American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

It has been revealed that as I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

Things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a new paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

This change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

According to recent reports, whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

In a recent development, trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is presently marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he remarked himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

Trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising fresh ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

It has been revealed that israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, announced wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

Industry observers note that israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

Without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

Sources indicate that it is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

In a recent development, israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s initiative for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

Recent findings suggest that israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

In a recent development, israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of new Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

Israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

These steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

If Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

Ronald Reagan Changed His Chief of Staff After a Midterm Trouncing, Too

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
  • While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

Recent findings suggest that but that’s not how Miller thinks, nor has it been Trump’s instinct. The Miller appointment stands in sharp contrast to the personnel change that then-President Ronald Reagan, the founding father of the conservative movement, made after the 1986 midterms and the scandal that broke out soon after. That year, Democrats regained control of the Senate (they had held the House since 1955), and the administration was embroiled in a major scandal that some Democrats believed could reach Watergate-like levels.

Sources indicate that the contrast between these two presidents reveals just how far Republican politics has radicalized since the 1980s. It is also a warning sign for Republicans who understand that, without a major course correction, the very same party that was celebrating a newly introduced governing coalition in 2024 might be on a self-destructive path. The GOP is in the grip of a strong leader who is not particularly interested in the long-term health of the party that brought him to the White House.

According to recent reports, reagan was not enjoying a good political moment in November 1986, though his presidency had been riding high until then. His first term was highly successful, featuring a historic supply-side tax cut and a vast acceleration of defense spending. He had defeated his opponent, former Vice President Walter Mondale, in a landslide victory in 1984. His approval ratings had been strong, and the economy had recovered from the malaise of the 1970s. In October 1986, Reagan signed bipartisan tax reform legislation that closed loopholes benefiting some of the nation’s most powerful interests, and he held a historic summit with the upcoming Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev.

But then came the 1986 midterms. Democrats gained five seats in the House, expanding their majority to 258, and, more importantly, retook control of the Senate by gaining eight seats. Their 55-seat majority ended the brief period of Republican control that had started with the 1980 election. The outcome was seen as a rebuke of the harsher edges of U.S. conservatism, as well the heightened tension with the Soviet Union that a hawkish Reagan had helped spur, despite two summits with Gorbachev. Indeed, the summit just weeks before voting in Reykjavik, Iceland, had broken down because the president refused to give up on his blueprint to build a missile shield around the United States, the Strategic Defense Initiative (which opponents dismissed as “star wars”). Soon after the election, Reagan’s problems deepened as news spread that a Lebanese magazine had reported that the United States had been secretly selling weapons to Iran.

Industry observers note that one of Reagan’s most significant moves in early 1987 was to replace his highly controversial chief of staff, Donald Regan. A former Marine and chairman of Merrill Lynch, Regan had been an crucial part of the Reagan administration since January 1981. As secretary of the Treasury, he had been instrumental in passing the 1981 tax cut. In February 1985, he became chief of staff, replacing James Baker (who replaced him at Treasury). Regan proved to be a forceful presence. He centralized control and pushed the president’s program in a highly aggressive and abrasive fashion that angered colleagues in the White House, as well as on Capitol Hill. The media did not find him very pleasant to work with, while first lady Nancy Reagan didn’t trust that he prioritized her husband’s interests.

With Regan by his side, Reagan’s first public response to what became the Iran-Contra scandal was defiance, which reflected his chief of staff’s approach to most problems. On Nov. 13, Reagan went on television to insist that there was nothing serious to investigate. While acknowledging that the White House had sold a small amount of “defensive” weapons to Iran as part of a major diplomatic initiative to build ties with moderates within the regime and combat terrorism, he denied that the United States had traded arms for hostages, or that the sales amounted to anything significant. Polls highlighted that the public was unconvinced that the president was telling the whole truth. Then, on Nov. 25, the other shoe dropped: Attorney General Edwin Meese revealed that profits from the weapons sales had been diverted to the anti-communist Nicaraguan Contras, despite the Boland Amendments’ congressional ban on such aid.

According to recent reports, privately, administration officials feared where the investigations were headed. For a generation that had watched Richard Nixon resign over Watergate just 12 years earlier, the possibility of impeachment seemed real. Reagan’s aides also understood that many voters had been shaped by those same memories, and were deeply distrustful of government officials and still insistent on a political system that could hold them accountable.

On Feb. 26, 1987, the president’s Special Review Board, a commission appointed by Reagan in November and headed by former Texas Sen. John Tower, issued its report on the Iran scandal. It blamed a chaotic management system that had allowed the arms sales and the diversion of funds to proceed, faulting Reagan’s leadership style and singling out Regan for failing to impose order on the White House. The next day, Regan resigned after learning that he was about to be relieved of his duties.

At this fraught moment, the president turned to Howard Baker.

The 61-year-old, mild-mannered Republican had served in the Senate from 1967 to 1985, the last four years as majority leader, and was respected on both sides of the aisle. He had been mentored by Senate Minority Leader Everett Dirksen (who was also his father-in-law), who taught him the ways and means of the legislative process and the art of bipartisan deal-making. Baker had gained national fame during the 1973 Watergate hearings by asking, “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Known as a moderate and an institutionalist, Baker was a selection widely seen as Reagan’s recognition that, with Democrats now controlling both chambers, he needed to build bridges to Capitol Hill rather than burn them. “I’d probably take some lumps from our right wingers but I can handle that,” Reagan noted in his diary, of appointing Baker.

Though Baker had actually been the third choice for chief of staff, he helped bring stability to the White House and guided the president through the Iran-Contra scandal. He brought in a first-rate team of advisors who improved relations with Congress, the press, and the first lady. Reagan biographers credit Baker with helping Reagan survive the scandal as the revelations mounted during the 1987 congressional hearings. He played a key role in brokering a budget deal with Congress after the October 1987 stock market crash and securing Senate ratification of the INF Treaty with the Soviet Union in May 1988. His tenure also had setbacks, most notably the Senate’s rejection of Robert Bork’s nomination to the Supreme Court. But his pragmatic outlook helped Reagan recover from the low of the 1986 midterms. “You always leave yourself a backdoor, a side door, and a trapdoor,” he liked to say, quoting something his father used to tell him. According to a longtime aide, that meant: “You don’t talk in absolutes. You don’t want to get yourself boxed in where you can’t maneuver.”.

Overall, Reagan and the first lady had reason to be pleased with Baker’s work: The president left office with high approval ratings—and helped bring an end to the Cold War.

In a recent development, today’s Republican Party is not your grandfather’s Republican Party, and the recent midterms suggested that much of the electorate is not happy with it. The reach of the Democratic victories into deeply red parts of the country, including Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas, suggests that the onetime party of Lincoln has a major problem on its hands. Part of that problem is the president himself, who after further radicalizing the GOP to its electoral detriment, highlights few signs that he will change course in ways that could strengthen the party that brought him to the dance.

With Miller as chief of staff, Trump is assuring voters that there will be more of the same style of politics and the same political agenda—leaving the Democratic Party with the kind of political prospects for united government that seemed impossible just a few months ago.

The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
  • Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
  • Recent findings suggest that turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

Recent findings suggest that turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

Turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a upcoming security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

This is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

Sources indicate that yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

It has been revealed that then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

It has been revealed that other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

Recent findings suggest that in this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara introduced the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

According to recent reports, some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “big, bold, and notable.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

It has been revealed that yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

Recent findings suggest that turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

In a recent development, furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

Sources indicate that some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

It has been revealed that ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK unveiled that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

In a recent development, turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

Industry observers note that today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

Sources indicate that the Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

Latest Update: The Democratic Party’s Three Conflicting Camps on AI

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

In a recent development, one way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Massive Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

One way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Massive Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

Sources indicate that to make gnarly matters more tangled, U.S. AI’s central player, Nvidia, has lost its co-founder and CEO over an alleged Chinese intelligence operation, scrambling all three impulses. And we should also remember that over at the White House, a bruised but belligerent Trump retains the executive levers and the veto—as well as an impulse to stymie whatever the Democrats wish to demonstrate as a “win” to the American public.

Before we get to Trump, though, let’s first consider what drives each of the camps in the Democratic coalition.

Industry observers note that the first camp can be thought of as the Restrainers. They want to check the proliferation of data centers while holding AI executives to account for independent testing of advanced models—and holding the companies liable for harm.

According to recent reports, midterm voters rewarded candidates in this camp, who pushed back on a sense that AI development was proceeding unchecked; Sherrod Brown won back an Ohio Senate seat with ads calling his opponent “the face of AI data centers,” while Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan also won races with opposition to data centers as a key element of their campaign platforms. In nine states, governors and governors-elect, too, have promised or imposed a pause on new data centers, stalling an estimated 41 percent of the country’s data center pipeline. Meanwhile, right after the elections, veteran Sen. Bernie Sanders called for a national data center moratorium.

While slowing down AI would be the most readily available and popular move by lawmakers, the Restrainers still have to get their house in order. They will need to prioritize the many risks and concerns around AI and focus their limited time on the most significant ones. Weighing these will not be easy. A household worried about its power bill, for instance, needs a different intervention compared with a parent who doesn’t want their child left alone with a chatbot.

A second camp is made up of the Riders. They have their eye on the economy and want to ensure that AI investments keep carrying U.S. growth, the stock market, and household retirement savings. AI has propped up the American economy in recent years; letting the air out of that balloon could produce a bust, a recession, and shrinking retirement accounts, which could be bad news come 2028 if voters lay the blame on Congress.

The sharp Nov. 5 reminder about the connection between AI growth and stock market growth is hard to ignore—right after the midterms results had sunk in, the S&P 500 stock index fell 4.4 percent, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff shock, led by stocks tied to the data center build-out, while the Nasdaq also had its deepest one-day drop in 19 months, with investors worried about tougher AI rules from a Democratic Congress.

The Riders will urge caution: hold the hearings, pass disclosure rules, but don’t touch the capital spending contributing to the economy and the stock market. Several moderate Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro or Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who are also presumed to be business-friendly, are considering presidential runs. They are likely to be the influential voices in the Riders camp.

Sources indicate that as for the third camp, let’s call them the Racers. These are Democrats who prioritize national security concerns and want to keep sensitive technology and advanced chips away from adversaries. Specifically, they are eager to ensure that China not win the AI race. The Racers have support from the likes of influential senators such as Elizabeth Warren and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer as well as post-midterms in-the-spotlight senators including James Talarico.

According to recent reports, while the AI race against China was not the concern that galvanized voters in the midterms and swept Democrats into Congress, a startling new development has the potential to make this a more pivotal political lever: the scandal involving Jensen Huang, who admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. This puts a spotlight on the extent to which China is keen to compete and centers the geopolitical stakes of the AI race in voters’ minds.

Huang’s abrupt exit from the organization that he co-founded puts wind at the backs of the Racers, especially with curbing chip sales to China becoming a rare cause with bipartisan support. But it also pushes the other camps to revise their agendas.

The Restrainers’ scrutiny of Big Tech’s leadership has national security implications. They will by now have realized that Nvidia did not have so much as a board chair until the day that Huang left—hardly a case for letting the industry police itself. For the Riders, with Nvidia as the load-bearer for the AI edifice, instability at the top could produce instability across the economy. They can point to half a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market value being lost within a few days of the scandal breaking and the board investigation beginning.

A Democratic coalition made up of these camps necessarily has a mix of divergent priorities. But while the legislative agenda will be set by political calculation, Congress can only guess at what a lame-duck president who controls the agencies, the veto, the export licenses, and his own stake in the AI trade will do in response.

Sources indicate that we have just had a preview: Even as a bipartisan chip bill is in process on Capitol Hill, the White House moved first, issuing its own rule to choke off China’s access to U.S. chips through data centers abroad.

Recent findings suggest that the public will vote again in two years, too short for politicians and too long for technologists. With all these conflicting forces in motion, I would argue that Congress needs to allocate its limited bandwidth to a prioritized short list of AI risks, such as those recorded in my own register of 103 documented cases.

Sources indicate that in the absence of a reconciliation across the divergent camps, the result could be a U.S. AI build-out that advances in fits and starts as deals get negotiated, an export regime that can swing with each hearing, a standoff between legislators on Capitol Hill and the White House, and allies who hedge because they cannot predict U.S. policy.

The Chinese AI industry would be handed the perfect case for promoting itself to the world as the comparable, trustworthy, and cheaper alternative. And it has managed to get to this point even without access to the most advanced chips that Huang himself had wanted to sell to them.

Meanwhile, to win, Beijing will not need a newly ascendant Democratic Party to pick the wrong camp. It only needs Washington to pick none.

It has been revealed that president Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. But lawmakers say his influence on Capitol Hill has already changed since Republicans’ midterm losses.

Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.

“In a few moments, under the immense powers vested in me by the Constitution of the United States of America, I will grant a full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever — to two magnificent Thanksgiving turkeys, special turkeys,” Trump said, suggesting he could extend his power to spare the birds from the holiday dining table to somehow grant them immortality.

While voters punished his party’s candidates for doing too little to address high prices and his decision to join Israel in going to war with Iran, Trump on Tuesday remained focused on another area of largely unchallenged authority — his White House projects. He began the event by touting the yearly event, for the first time, being held on the helipad he had built on the White House’s South Lawn. Later, he revealed prepares for another newly introduced location next year.

“I'm told that per the long-running tradition, these exquisite animals stayed overnight at the nearby Willard Hotel. Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodation to host such distinguished guests,” he noted of the turkeys. “I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built. It's going to host a lot of people and a couple of turkeys next year. We're going to do it inside.”.

Recent findings suggest that trump also highlighted that the two bright, white turkeys were raised in West Virginia — which he carried more than 40 points when he was on the ballot. The turkeys, now spared, will spend their remaining years in Texas, a state where Democrats scored two of their most high profile wins in the House and Senate races — something Trump left unmentioned.

In a recent development, the pre-holiday vibes were lighthearted on Tuesday, with the president slated to later travel to South Florida for a Thanksgiving weekend of turkey and time at one of his golf clubs. But when he returns, lawmakers will continue assessing how much sway he still has on Capitol Hill as he begins what, for his predecessors, were their lame-duck eras.

One Republican Senate ally acknowledged his influence with lawmakers already has changed.

“I think it's going to be policy-to-policy on that,” said Senate Republican Conference Vice Chair James Lankford.

Industry observers note that “But he's the president of the United States all the way to the very end. So he still has his veto pen,” the Oklahoman added. “He still has the ability to be able to direct agencies to engage. We're passing legislation. It takes three to tango: House, Senate, and the White House.”.

Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz of Texas stated Trump’s influence, once the Democrat-controlled House and Senate are seated on Jan. 3, “will, obviously, be different.”.

“I don't think the incoming Democrat majorities are interested in passing productive legislation and passing pro-jobs legislation,” said Cruz, a potential 2028 GOP presidential candidate. “I think, instead, they're just going to attack the president all day long.”.

Still, Cruz predicted “the president will continue to lead.”.

Trump on Monday showed how he likely intends to use his lame-duck influence on and off Capitol Hill when he successfully pushed for the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. During an interview with CNBC’s Eamon Javers, Trump made an admission that would be stunning from any other sitting American president about a private organization, saying he had been “speaking to the board directly and indirectly.”.

In a Monday statement, Nvidia noted its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Sources indicate that such unprecedented moves are a significant reason why Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., last week remarked he expects Trump to be Trump — despite overseeing a midterms campaign he insisted be about himself and his unpopular second-term record.

In a recent development, “Any president is going to have a lot of influence because they get to run the executive branch,” noted Scott, a former Sunshine State chief executive. “And they have the biggest pulpit in the world. So he's going to continue to have a lot of influence.”.

Still, some Republican lawmakers have criticized Trump and his team for what they call recent stumbles.

Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana last week told reporters he had “a lot of questions” about how Trump and his administration handled upgrades to the country’s air traffic control system that prompted a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13.

“Somebody needs to be held accountable for what happened,” he said, raising concerns about the president demanding $50 billion in additional taxpayer monies to build a new system. “I’m not fully convinced that throwing out more money is going to solve the fundamental problems.”.

Trump also has taken ample friendly fire on social media from GOP members over his interference in the Huang scandal.

In a recent development, north Carolina GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan took to X to say the Nvidia founder’s reinstatement was “a mistake.”.

“For the past two years, I have privately said there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised. Turns out, well, we all know,” Harrigan wrote after Trump contended an administration probe had “exonerated” Huang of any potential wrongdoing. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the manufacturer and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.”.

Harrigan, a rare Tar Heel State Republican incumbent to win another term, echoed other GOP lawmakers in calling for an in-depth congressional probe in the Huang scandal and his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Next week could offer an early test of other Republicans’ willingness to break more publicly with Trump on certain challenges, as Huang is scheduled to appear before multiple congressional committees.

Even before Trump threw his political weight behind Huang’s return, Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said he had sensed a GOP president who had lost clout with his party’s Senate conference.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the Nvidia concern has caused some major concerns about the Trump China policy, obviously,” Kaine stated. “That is definitely creating some anxiety.”.

Trump has given clues that he is as concerned with his influence among the incoming Democratic majorities.

In a recent development, “If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too,” Trump said during a Friday press conference at the White House. “You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with.”.
